View synthesis in video prediction involves forecasting a new view of the scene from a different vantage point. The challenge lies in the fact that the video frames captured from various angles are not directly correlated. A common approach to this problem involves creating a dual representation of the image, with one representation focused on detailed local information and the other on the overall scene layout. We propose using two separate networks for each representation, with a shared cross-representation encoder. Each representation's network uses a respective encoder, situated at the opposite end of the pipeline. We tested this dual representation framework on the NVIE view synthesis dataset, demonstrating that it yields a higher PSNR score compared to the baseline multi-view video codec.

In multi-level systems, inter-level coupling can result in an entangled state of
different energy levels, and this coupling can be as strong as intra-level
excitations. We demonstrate the significant coupling between the ground level and
the first excited level of a two-photon system by analyzing the correlation of
their creation/annihilation operators. This coupling allows for the creation of
a single inter-level quasi-particle and we show that it can be observed in the
intensity correlation function of a multi-mode light field. Furthermore, we show
that this coupling can be utilized to achieve an inter-level atom-field entanglement.

The Ω-baryon, a diquark-triquet system with the unique property of having only anomalous electric charge, has been extensively studied in various theoretical models. Due to its special properties, this particle is expected to have unique behavior under external perturbations. To gain insight into its internal structure, we performed a detailed theoretical analysis of the Ω-baryon's spectrum using the relativistic quark model, considering the effects of the glue and sea quarks within the Hadron's structure. By comparing our findings with available experimental data, we determined the parameters that describe the quark's internal structure and their contributions to the Hadron's mass spectrum. In addition, we calculated the electromagnetic form factors of the Ω-baryon at various momentum transfers to gain further understanding of its internal structure.

Understanding and modeling the airflow within vehicles are crucial for creating effective disinfection strategies in public transportation, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. While previous studies have analyzed air exchange dynamics in aircraft and office spaces, this study utilizes computational fluid dynamics and tracer gas simulations to analyze air movement in a bus. By comparing their results to a widely adopted model of convection, the study highlights the significance of accounting for localized turbulence and heat transfer when predicting disease transmission on urban buses. Furthermore, they propose a set of guidelines for creating more accurate models of convective mixing in vehicles based on their design and the presence of obstacles.

The proposed experiment aims to directly observe the quantized fluctuations of an electric field in a vacuum, specifically its diffractive and birefringent characteristics, by investigating the interaction of x-ray photons with an electrostatic field in a crystal. To enhance the likelihood of successful detection, we are analyzing various signal extraction methods and assessing their sensitivity to the proposed experimental parameters. Adjusting parameters such as the size of a beam filter, the thickness of a crystal layer, and the characteristics of a x-ray spectrum can significantly impact the detection of the desired effect. We found that detecting the birefringent difference in x-ray photon splitting that occurs when interacting with an electrostatic field in a (110) silicon crystal requires a beam filter size of approximately one micron in order to exceed the proposed experiment's background threshold. Additionally, we found that a thinner silicon layer (around 100 nanometers) is necessary in order to minimize the absorption of x-rays and their own splitting signals. Furthermore, we found that a mid-spectra photon energy is more susceptible to the desired effect and better detects the birefringent difference in x-ray photon splitting.

In 1881, Karl Wilhelm Eisenlohr developed a theoretical approach to standardize polyhedron translations. Eighty-five years later, in 1946, Frank Farris built upon this work, resulting in a method that ensures the transitive property across all faces of a polyhedron. This article will delve into the history of their collaboration and provide an in-depth examination of the Eisenlohr-Farris method. Additionally, we will utilize 3D printing to create various polyhedra based on their developments.

Uncloneable encryption is a technique that utilizes an untrusted server to distribute encrypted messages to multiple recipients, even if the server has access to previous encrypted communications between the users and the server. Our work presents enhanced uncloneable encryption schemes using two types of weakly reliable functions: one type that produces distinct, non-identity outputs for identical inputs, and another that generates unique outputs for distinct inputs. We also explored uncloneable encryption in the presence of a malicious server that can manipulate encrypted data. To achieve this, we defined a new type of weakly reliable function that produces the original input when given a specific modified input, and developed a method for producing uncloneable encryption using this type of function.

This paper introduces a novel concept called "unkeyed verification," which involves determining whether a given encrypted message was transmitted over a specific noise-prone communication channel, without access to the actual transmission or any additional information beyond the received encrypted data. Unkeyed verification goes beyond the traditional goals of keyless cryptography, such as keyless encryption detection and code decoding, as it aims to verify the authenticity of the transmission regardless of any potential errors caused by channel noise. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of unkeyed verification in Gaussian noise-prone channels, and demonstrate that it is theoretically impossible if the level of noise is known. However, we also identify a specific threshold below which unkeyed verification becomes possible, and develop a practical approach using statistical analysis to verify the transmission in cases where the noise level is unknown.

We've examined the electronic and plasmonic characteristics of doped, twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides using a tight-binding model and their long-wave-length limits. Our analysis reveals that these materials exhibit flat-band physics similar to those seen in excitonic states found in microcavity systems. This flat band gives rise to a long-lived, spatially localized plasmon mode with an oscillation period equivalent to that of the lattice constant. The longevity of this plasmon is maintained down to relatively high doping levels, primarily due to the reduced scattering from long-wave-length fluctuations in the material. This unique property could be utilized to develop high-quality plasmon resonators for applications in quantum computing and other related fields.

This paper aims to investigate an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton $\tilde{g}$ obtained from a Sasakian manifold $(M, g)$. We establish the connection between $\tilde{g}$ and the original metric $g$ and prove that the soliton $\tilde{g}$ is conformal to $g$, i.e., $\tilde{g} = \phi^2 g$ for a smooth function $\phi$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the potential function $\phi$ associated with $\tilde{g}$ is constant if and only if the potential function $f$ associated with $g$ is constant. Furthermore, we show that if the soliton $\tilde{g}$ is conformal to $g$, then $f$ and $\phi$ are related by $f = c\phi$ for a non-zero constant $c$.

Both celestial objects and planets can experience the devastating effects of erosive energy, being stripped of their atmospheric layers due to powerful magnetic fields from wind-generated currents or direct high-energy radiation, or being engulfed by the gravitational pull of the stars they revolve around, suffering an even more tragic fate. In the case of planets, a similar, yet distinct phenomenon occurs, where they are consumed by the intense heat of their own stars, undergoing a process known as tidal heating. Both processes can induce mass loss, atmospheric loss, and heating in magnetized objects, whether they are planets or stars. Understanding the complex interactions between these objects' magnetic fields, atmospheres, and the surrounding environments requires a multidisciplinary approach that draws from the fields of astrophysics, planetary science, and geophysics. Recent breakthroughs in numerical modeling, observational data, and laboratory experiments have significantly expanded our knowledge of these processes, but there remain many unanswered questions about the behavior of winds, magnetospheres, and the interactions between stars and planets.

The spin-orbit proximity effect is a phenomenon where a strong spin-orbit interaction in one material influences the spin dynamics in another material, typically occurring in a proximity layer. In our research, we examined the proximity effect in multilayered Bi/Co films with varying thicknesses of both Bi and Co. Our findings indicate that the Bi proximity effect in Co is influenced by two factors: the intrinsic properties of Bi and its interface with Co. When the Bi thickness is less than 2 nm, the Bi proximity effect in Co follows an exponential decay, while thicker Bi layers exhibit a 1/distance behavior. Additionally, our data suggest that the Bi/Co interface has a strong spin-orbit interaction that contributes to the Bi proximity effect in Co. These results provide a comprehensive understanding of the spin-orbit proximity effect in multilayered Bi/Co films.

This paper tackles the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalized Mie-type potential. The potential generalization reads $V(a,b,c,d,r^{a/d})=Me^{2a/r^{a/d}}/r^{b/c}$, and we obtain a precise solution using the Jumarie type fractional derivative. Our approach involves transforming the fractional Schrödinger equation into an exact differential equation via the substitution $f(r)=(r^{d}/\phi(d))\,_{J}D^{a}_{r}r^{a/d}$, where $\phi(d)$ is a fractional integration property. We then solve the resulting exact differential equation to obtain the corresponding energy eigenvalue equation. Notably, our research extends earlier works on the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation for the Mie-type potential by adjusting the dimensions and using the Jumarie type fractional derivative.

We analyzed various regularizations used in neural networks, including enforcing Lipschitz continuity, and found this specific approach to be effective in preventing the network from learning unnecessary patterns. By capping the neural network's ability to amplify input differences, we investigated how different constraints on the network's weights impact its performance. We discovered that the L1 regularization, which is uncommon in neural network training, can lead to a more stable and less overfitting-prone model when compared to traditional L2 regularization. However, it ultimately results in a less optimal model. We also explored alternative methods of achieving similar outcomes with greater efficiency.

Sequential neural network models like LSTMs are capable of complex pattern recognition, however, analysis of their application to studying sentence structure in Basque reveals that they are not utilizing their full potential for syntactic analysis. Analysis of both sentence classification and fully-supervised tree extraction tasks indicates that the benefits of using a sequential LSTM model over a feed-forward one is minimal, suggesting that the simple word-by-word pattern used by the latter is sufficient for these tasks. Furthermore, examination of the learned representations within the sequential model reveals that any benefits it offers are largely confined to the surface level, and that it is primarily utilizing local features such as part-of-speech and word position to make predictions.

HD80606b, a planet that orbits a G-type star, presents a unique opportunity to study planet-atmosphere interactions due to its extreme 648-hour orbital period and significant 43-degree tilt. Observations of the planet as it passes in front of its star are crucial for determining its atmospheric properties. However, its highly eccentric orbit causes challenges in scheduling such observations. A recent transit observation near periastron failed to match the predicted time, highlighting the need for a more precise orbital calendar. To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of multiple transit observations using a global network of telescopes, including the Kepler space telescope. By employing a sophisticated modeling technique, we calculated the planet's orbital period to be 647.96 days, its eccentricity to be 0.93, and its transit periods near periastron and apastron to be 3.14 and 87.3 hours respectively. Our findings have a 1% margin of error and confirm the planet's unusual behavior. To make the most out of the James Webb Space Telescope, we recommend scheduling observations for transit epochs near apastron to increase the likelihood of detecting the planet's atmosphere during this more pronounced transit phenomenon.

Foundations games, such as Tetris, achieve high player engagement while providing a gentle introduction to gameplay mechanics. Research into the cognitive benefits of foundations games suggests they can be a valuable tool for physical rehabilitation, helping patients make progress through a combination of mental motivation and physical therapy. However, the long-term sustainability of games like Tetris is hindered by their difficulty, which can lead to frustration and game abandonment. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a method for predictive game design, which uses mathematical models to analyze game content and identify optimal starting points for players based on their individual skill levels. To apply this approach to foundations games for rehabilitation, we've developed a suite of mathematical models tailored to this game type. These models enable the creation of personalized gameplay experiences that adapt to a player's performance, providing a motivating and challenging experience that can help players make progress and maintain engagement over time.

This research proposes a variational approach, utilizing a gradient flow, to estimate functionals defined on piecewise-rigid maps within a given domain. The method involves introducing a phase-field parameter to represent an implicit area dividing the map into rigid components within the given domain. The proposed approach uses this implicit division to simplify the definition of the functional as one that can be directly optimized through a variation of the flow. The approach also allows for the use of the phase-field to optimize a related area-functional that can be linked to the original functional through a flow. The research establishes the existence and uniqueness of a minimum for the proposed variational problem, as well as the convergence of a discrete scheme. The method has the advantage of being able to handle non-smooth and convex components of the piecewise-rigid map. The research also investigates the relationship between the proposed variational approach and a conventional piecewise-rigid model.

We investigate the production of lepton-neutrino pairs via Drell-Yan processes within third-generation vector leptoquark models at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Utilizing the flexible NLO+PS tool, MadGraph5_mCF (MG5_mcF), in conjunction with the ColliderFlow (CF) package, we obtain accurate cross-section calculations at next-to-leading order in QCD. To complement these findings, we also examine the possible decay paths of these leptoquarks to hadrons, calculating the associated cross-sections at next-to-leading order in QCD for a range of masses and couplings. These studies are carried out for the LHC operating at a variety of energy and luminosity settings. To facilitate the incorporation of these results into existing experimental analyses, we provide a set of precomputed acceptance criteria based on a comprehensive set of final-state hadronic configurations. These studies are being conducted in anticipation of the LHC's potential discovery of vector leptoquarks, and the associated Drell-Yan production of lepton-neutrino pairs will likely play a significant role in the subsequent interpretation of the data.

We've integrated an important physical consideration into PET image reconstruction, neglected in conventional optimization methods, to account for the image intensity constraints. To address this, we've developed an uncertainty-aware neural network that takes into consideration the variance of training data, to prevent it from being biased by unrealistic assumptions. The network uses two separate branches to process PET and dosimeter readings for different input intensities, and incorporates a variance loss function to adapt to variations in training data. To prevent it from being sensitive to abnormal data during testing, we've added a neural network barrier function, to provide a regularization effect through the interaction between the two branches. The proposed method has been evaluated using synthetic data and clinical scans, and has shown improved results in terms of quantitative metrics and visual quality compared to conventional methods, including analytical reconstruction, deep learning, and robust learning.

Online advertisements are tailored to users based on their browsing history, with the objective of increasing sales and effectiveness. This research aims to gauge the impact of online tracking on consumers' perceptions and willingness to engage with personalized advertisements. A survey revealed significant differences in how much individuals value personalized ads, with some finding them appealing and others being indifferent or even disliking them. Interestingly, the study discovered a notable subset of participants who expressed a preference for personalized ads, even when given the option to opt out of online tracking. This phenomenon was interpreted as these participants deriving utility from personalized ads, which are funded through online advertising revenue. To examine this aspect further, the study included a secondary survey that explored participants' awareness and concerns about online data collection and tracking. The results showed a notable disparity between participants' knowledge and concerns regarding online tracking, with a substantial majority being aware of data collection but expressing lower concerns about it.

This paper delves into the analysis of the relationship between centering theory and coreference resolution using neural networks. It begins by outlining the principles of centering theory and its components, before presenting a coreference resolution evaluation using the Automatic Evaluation of Coreference Resolution (ACE) metric. The study examines the correlation between coreference evaluation metrics and centering theory's sub-theories, including cataphoricity, center distribution status, and nuclear status. The evaluation includes a detailed breakdown of these correlations for each sub-theory. The study also compares the performance of a strong neural coreference resolution system with a model that incorporates centering theory, but found no improvement in the evaluation metrics. The research concludes with discussions on potential limitations of the evaluation methods and the potential implications of the study's findings for future work on coreference resolution.

We have developed a set of parameters that reduce the complexity of the Upward Planarity Testing problem. Specifically, we analyzed the impact of ordering edges by their endpoints' x-coordinates, removing edges based on a specific set, and partitioning the graph's vertices into distinct subsets. Through this parameterization, we were able to solve the upward planarity testing problem in polynomial time under certain conditions, including but not limited to: (1) restricting the graph to a single-concept family known as "K_4-free" graphs, (2) limiting the number of edges to a small, fixed quantity (e.g. NLOGSPACE boundary), and (3) dividing the graph into isolated subgraphs following a specific structure. Moreover, we established an efficient algorithm (i.e. nearly linear time) for embedding upward trees in 3D space.

The rise of complex, high-performance computing systems in various fields like artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and scientific simulations has created significant challenges for both individual and enterprise users. These systems often comprise numerous nodes, each requiring configuration, leading to a tedious and error-prone setup process. To streamline this process, a system setup framework is proposed that automates the configuration of large computing clusters across multiple platforms. This framework leverages a modular architecture to accommodate various third-party tools and libraries, enabling it to handle the intricacies of configuring complex computing systems. To facilitate easy integration, a module development guide has been created, covering the essential steps to develop a cluster automation module using Python. This proposed framework has been successfully applied in an enterprise context, demonstrating its capability to handle large-scale computing cluster setups.

We investigated the relationship between two theories that describe quantum operator growth: the qKLS (quenched Kardar-Parisi-Zhang-Landers) model and the SYK model. We studied this relationship in two areas: (1) the average half-chain operator complexity and (2) the distribution of operator complexity in the quenching scenario. For both cases, we used both unitary evolution and the quantum circuit construction. Our calculations showed that the behavior of operator complexity varies depending on the number of quanta $n$, with two distinct phases of description: in the small $n$ regime, the distribution is consistent with the qKLS model, while in the large $n$ regime, the distribution is consistent with the SYK model. This duality was observed in both the average operator complexity and the distribution of operator complexity under quenching.

This paper presents a WiFi-based range estimation algorithm utilizing supervised machine learning, with the aim of minimizing the need for extensive measurements typically required in conventional distance estimation methods. The proposed system leverages a machine learning model to predict distances based on the characteristics of radio signal strength. In testing the algorithm with real data, a notable improvement in accuracy was observed, with mean errors as low as 12 centimeters. The code and data utilized in this research are freely available online.

The vast majority of supermassive black holes reside in the heart of galaxies that are actively forming stars, yet it's unclear why these black holes aren't consumed by the surrounding starlight. It's possible that a complex system of dust and nanoparticles, created through a process known as Dyson Sphere formation, is absorbing and utilizing the energy from nearby stars. In a new theoretical framework, we explore the possibility of a shell-like structure composed of dust and nanoparticles being used for energy absorption, and demonstrate that it could maintain its stability in close proximity to a star. To apply this concept to a broader range of scenarios, we performed a set of general relativistic simulations focusing on a shell consisting of dust and nanoparticles surrounding a black hole that is accreting matter. The results reveal that the shell can withstand the tidal forces generated by the black hole, and maintain its stability even when facing stars that are up to 10% of the mass of the sun. In such cases, the shells can orbit the stars at the same rate as the stars' rotation, allowing them to harness energy from the stars' magnetic fields. In order to fully utilize the energy from nearby stars, the shell would need to be able to withstand external forces, and could potentially be stabilized through its own internal magnetic field. Network applications rely heavily on service-based architectures, which are under pressure to perform optimally in an increasingly crowded internet environment. A crucial component of these services is the SLA, which outlines the expected performance standards. Efficient monitoring of these standards in real-time across a distributed network is a significant challenge. This paper explores the potential benefits of using a P2P system to detect SLA breaches in real-time. We discuss how a P2P system can provide a more comprehensive view of network performance by gathering data from nodes, which enables the early detection of standard violations. We also examine two possible approaches to implementing this in a P2P system and analyze the performance standards required for each. Finally, we discuss possible applications and the potential for adapting this to detect breaches in other performance standards.

The beam breakup instability caused by the regeneration section in energy recovery linacs poses a problem that could hinder efficient energy recovery. Although studies have identified potential causes and countermeasures, the issue remains unsolved. This paper aims to examine the role of filling pattern on beam breakup instability by comparing simulations using different patterns, which could provide insights for designing fill patterns to minimize beam-beam interactions and thus reduce beam breakup instability.

To operate the CS2 detector in the CS2 neutron scattering experiment at the LANSCE HIE, it's crucial to determine the total cross-section of neutrons scattering off carbon atoms. This cross-section was measured at a 632.8 nm wavelength using a 264.5 nanosecond pulsed neutron beam with a peak flux of 2.5 x 10^8 neutrons per square centimeter per second. The measurement was taken using a novel 3D scintillator sensor with 50 millimeter long and 50 millimeter wide pixels, where the scintillator's luminescence was analyzed in three dimensions. The measured cross-section was found to be 5.73 x 10^-2 barns per carbon atom at a 0.98 eV electron volts equivalent, which is consistent with other measurements using other detectors and a Monte Carlo simulation using the MCNP6 code.

In a previous series of experiments, we found that particles made of a mixture of organic and silicate materials demonstrated a strong affinity for sticking together as temperatures rose from 300K to 800K. This tendency to adhere persisted even when subjected to impacts exceeding 10 meters per second. In the current study, we expand on this research by introducing a higher fraction of water into the particles, observing how this alteration affects their sticking properties as temperatures change. In the experiments conducted at room temperature, the particles with a higher water content showed a significantly reduced tendency to adhere following high-speed collisions. This distinction in behavior highlights the potential discrepancy in dust sticking properties as temperatures vary, which could be utilized to explain the observed discrepancies in particle sizes within various planetary formation zones. In particular, this phenomenon may shed light on the difficulties in forming particles in the inner regions of protoplanetary discs, particularly those rich in water, and may also provide a reason for the observed discrepancies in particle sizes in the hot inner regions of discs even in the presence of growth through accretion.

The Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is an adaptation of the Fisher Discriminant Analysis (FDA) tailored for handling high-dimensional, overlapped, and noisy data sets. By applying a technique similar to PCA, LFDA overcomes FDA's dimensional constraints, allowing for the identification of discriminant components that transform data into low-dimensional spaces while highlighting class differences. The lfda R package executes both standard LFDA and Renes et al.'s (2019) simplified methods, incorporating visualization capabilities via 3D plotting.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robotics to quickly
acquire complex skills from expert demonstrations. While successful in many
scenarios, imitation learning faces significant challenges when the task has
nonlinear constraints, involves adapting to new situations, and requires
avoiding obstacles not present in the training data. To overcome these
obstacles, we introduce a generalized imitation learning framework (EKMP) to
learn new skills efficiently. EKMP incorporates multiple nonlinear constraints
and adapts to new environments based on the expert's policy, obtained from
demonstrations with soft constraints. To handle hard and soft constraints
simultaneously, we developed a novel two-time-scale framework, allowing us
to efficiently learn the policy by utilizing stochastic gradient descent on a
projected space. Theoretical analysis of the proposed framework provides a
biological plausibility, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by achieving
human-like performance on challenging tasks such as navigating through tight
gaps and adapting to new environments with tight constraints, on multiple
robotic platforms.

This paper presents the one-loop central-emission vertex for two gluons in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, confirming the equivalence of the supergravity approximation and the full quantum field theory computation.

We've analyzed the Rashba Hubbard model with an attractive interaction on a Harper-Hofstadter lattice, subject to an external magnetic field. A Rashba interaction creates a non-trivial lattice structure, which can be mapped to a triangular lattice in the weak field limit. In this limit, a mean-field approximation reveals that a spin-polarized phase gives way to a non-spin-polarized phase as the Rashba interaction strength increases. Notably, this non-spin-polarized phase exhibits topological characteristics and can be understood through a weak-field weak-coupling expansion. This phase is separated from a spin-polarized phase that can be described by a Feshbach scenario by a Rashba interaction strength, which can be manipulated through optical lattice techniques. The requirements for achieving the topological non-spin-polarized phase include aligning the magnetic field with the lattice structure and using a specific ratio of Rashba interaction to magnetic flux.

In the vicinity of a strong magnetic field, a superconductor's vortex lattice undergoes a complex transformation, influenced by both its intrinsic properties and the external field. A recent theoretical framework suggests that near a high-field point, the vortex lattice transition can change from a square to a triangular arrangement due to the interplay of pinning forces and electromagnetic interactions. However, identifying this transition has been a challenge, primarily because the associated changes are often very subtle and difficult to detect directly. In this study, we employed a combination of resistivity and Hall effect measurements under high magnetic fields to investigate the behavior of a vortex lattice in the superconductor Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+x}$. By analyzing the Hall effect in this system, we found a non-linear response that is closely related to the orientation of the vortex lattice. This allowed us to use a different approach to detect the square-to-triangular transition, which we found to occur at a specific high-field point, closely aligned with the predicted behavior. This finding highlights the importance of considering the vortex lattice's orientation in the Hall effect and provides a more direct means of detecting the square-to-triangular transition transition.

The highly extended, melted state of a grafted polymer brush is re-examined, and a new approach is developed which focuses on the concept of an "exclusion area" outside of the grafts. Unlike previous methods, this approach disregards the idea of an "exclusion zone" within the grafts. Instead, the excluded volume is directly measured by analyzing the distribution of a free polymer within the molten brush. In contrast to traditional theories, the excluded volume is found to be greater than the volume of the inner "exclusion area" within the grafts. Furthermore, the distribution of a free polymer within the molten brush is used to derive an analytical expression for the excluded volume outside of the grafts. In the case of a semi-space, this excluded volume is equivalent to half the volume of the excluded area.

In this study, we introduce a new concept called trimmed metric dimension, which builds upon the existing metric dimension framework. Initially, we provide theoretical guidelines for determining the trimmed metric dimension of a graph. Notably, we develop an algorithmic approach to calculate the trimmed dimension of a graph by removing a specified number of landmark vertices. We then investigate various scenarios, including the computation of minimum and maximum trimmed dimension, as well as the trimmed dimension of graph projections. Furthermore, we introduce the notion of trimmed dimension for dynamic graphs. In addition to theoretical insights, we conducted an experimental analysis of the trimmed dimension of different real-world graphs under different landmark trimming scenarios.

The Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi LAT) has been monitoring the sky in the gamma-ray band for over a decade, yielding an enormous dataset that includes numerous sources, as well as unidentified features in its all-sky maps. To extract more information from its vast dataset of observations, machine learning algorithms can be trained on the data and used to create a new all-sky map highlighting the most significant sources, including those that change over time, for further study. This paper outlines the framework for such an approach, using a random forest classifier that distinguishes genuine sources from fake ones, and investigates how the model's performance is affected by its parameters, such as the number of features used and the number of training data points. The paper also presents all-sky maps created using a model that has been optimized for accuracy, and compares its results to previous analyses, including a catalog of sources released by the Fermi LAT Collaboration in 2020, and to a more recent analysis that used a different approach. The paper also discusses the implications of using machine learning algorithms on the Fermi LAT dataset, including the potential for discovering sources that change over time, and the advantages of using such algorithms for future telescopes and datasets.

In the context of graph theory, a serial dictatorship mechanism is a method of making mutually exclusive and irrevocable choices from a set of options by multiple self-interested agents, where the order of the agents' selections is predetermined. If the order doesn't align with the preferences, alternative mechanisms like the 'dictatorship of choice' may be more effective, but this could potentially undermine the original order of selections. Under the assumption that agents act rationally and make rational decisions based on expected outcomes, we investigate how the order of selections can be strategically chosen to achieve a particular outcome. Our analysis yields conditions under which a fixed order of selections is optimal, as well as methods for identifying the largest subset of agents whose preferred order of selections is unaffected by their individual self-interest. We refer to such a stable order of selections as a'serial monarchy'. We also explore the conditions under extending this concept to other mechanisms like the 'liberal dictatorship' and 'plural voting'.

We have developed a new method for detecting binary asters (Mira stars with periodic
maxima) using data from the Pan-STARRS1 Sky Survey. This technique involves
identifying similar stars to a sample Mira star and estimating the binary aster's light
variation period. We used this method to analyze 1,500 randomly selected Mira stars
from the General Catalogue of Variable Stars and validated our results against the
ASAS-SN database of variable stars. For a light curve period less than 62 days, our
results matched 95% of the entries from the GCVS and 85% of the ASAS-SN data. For
light curve periods greater than 62 days, our results matched 85% of the entries from
the GCVS and 60% of the ASAS-SN data. We also used this method to search for
binary asters in the Pan-STARRS1 database and found 1,200 candidates with periods
greater than 62 days. We plan to use this method to search for binary asters in the
Pan-STARRS1 database in regions near the Galactic Plane, which we anticipate will
yield 3,000 to 5,000 candidates.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer influence within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study formulates a revised version of Leibniz's Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. To maintain consistency, we also adapt product, chain, and d'Alembert's Rules for (VL)Riemann-Liouville fractional operators. Furthermore, specific examples are provided to illustrate the application of these modified rules.

This paper analyzes the performance of a linear detection method, using the recursive least squares algorithm, in identifying signals that change across space. It is assumed that the detection device acquires data from different locations, varying continuously over a range. The investigation focuses on an ideal scenario where data is collected under optimal conditions and an exact model is known. It is shown that the accuracy of the detection method improves as the rate at which data is collected increases, within certain limits. It is also demonstrated that the optimal collection rate that yields the highest accuracy decreases as the level of noise increases. Furthermore, two scenarios are analyzed in which the signals that change across space follow specific patterns. It is found that certain patterns allow for higher collection rates than others. It is also shown that the detection method can be applied in real-world situations, such as identifying moving targets using radar systems.

Researchers in astrophysics and planetary science rely heavily on visualizations of data, whether it's imaging, spectral, or other formats, to effectively communicate their findings to a broader audience and facilitate discussion within the field. To address this need, we've developed a suite of open-source, customizable web visualizers that allow users to interactively explore their data, including 2D and 3D imaging, 1D and 2D spectral data, as well as time-series and phase-folded diagrams. These visualizers are part of the RCSED project, a comprehensive resource for the MAST database hosted by NED, and are available for public use at the project website.

The Southern Atlantic rift opened around 120 million years ago, during the Cretaceous period, as Africa and South America moved apart. Researchers have studied the movement of Africa and South America since then, analyzing how the two continents continued to drift apart and eventually took on their current shapes. In the process, the Central Atlantic magmatic province was formed, with massive volcanic eruptions occurring on both sides of the rift. The volcanic activity ceased once the rift had developed a central oceanic basin. In contrast, the Southern Atlantic rift experienced ongoing magmatic activity, with volcanic eruptions occurring in a linear pattern on the African side, particularly in present-day Brazil and Uruguay. These volcanic eruptions were likely caused by the movement of tectonic plates, which created areas of stress in the Earth's crust. As a result, the volcanic eruptions in these areas continued for an extended period. In the case of the Brazilian-Uruguayan volcanic eruptions, they ceased once the rift had developed a more asymmetrical shape, with the African side stretching more than the South American side. In the process, the volcanic eruptions in these areas became tilted at a 10-degree angle. In order to understand the early history of the Southern Atlantic rift, researchers have studied the shape of the volcanic eruptions in these areas, particularly in the Brazilian-Uruguayan region. By analyzing the geometry of these volcanic eruptions, they have reconstructed the movement of Africa and South America since the rift opened, and have

A proven approach to enhancing segmentation models using unlabelled data is through unsupervised training, particularly contrastive learning. Despite its effectiveness, this method typically relies on random data augmentations, which can be limiting due to the small number of possible transformations, especially when working with medical images. Additionally, the model often focuses on easily transformable regions, neglecting those that are boundary-sensitive. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a novel framework that leverages unlabeled data for training, targeting the maximization of information in areas that are challenging to segment due to their sensitivity to image boundaries. Specifically, the model is designed to learn from unlabelled data by prioritizing the boundary-sensitive regions that are difficult to distinguish between different classes. To achieve this, the model uses a score that identifies such regions based on their proximity to object boundaries, obtained through the analysis of medical images. To prevent the model from focusing solely on easily transformable boundary-sensitive regions, the model incorporates multiple data augmentations to capture a diverse range of such regions. To validate the proposed framework, experiments were conducted using two publicly available datasets for cardiac and liver segmentation, with the results showing that it outperforms the baseline model using supervised training and other self-supervised training methods.

Introducing an artificial intelligence dungeon master, part of an open-source framework called D4D, which enables natural language interactions to guide players through tabletop role-playing games like Dungeons and Dragons. D4D's AI dungeon master includes a unique set of elements, such as a theory-of-mind component and a pre-existing dataset of game data, that allow it to learn from various sources of information, including natural language interactions. To train this AI to effectively manage conversations, D4D uses a specialized approach that involves identifying game-related intents and leveraging a set of pre-defined theory-of-mind rules to create a more human-like understanding of the players' perspectives. By doing so, the AI becomes capable of engaging in complex role-playing games, as evidenced by its ability to successfully complete challenging quests in the popular video game Dungeons of Dreadful Silence. According to human evaluations, the AI dungeon master's performance is not only comparable to a human-controlled version of the game but also surpasses it in several key areas.

Large-scale lexical resources, such as word embeddings, contain the inherent structure of a language, making them an ideal basis for innovative methods of discovery. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on predefined metrics, our proposed framework uses multivariate statistical analysis to uncover hidden patterns within the data. By applying it to the semantic space of German words, our results show that it can identify categories that other methods miss, such as words associated with the level of inference, and even discover new patterns of negation.

We propose a new set of distribution functions that depend on the transverse relative momentum of particles, $k_\perp$, in accordance with the WIMY approach. This framework correctly accounts for collinear divergences that arise in relativistic quantum field theories, often handled through the zeta function trick. Our proposed distribution functions can be applied to describe hard-scattering processes within QCD, and are defined by a set of functions that include the well-known Bose-Einstein distribution, $f_B$, as well as others such as $f_2$, $f_3$, and $f_4$, which can be expressed in terms of $k_\perp$-dependent quasi-distributions of parton densities. We demonstrate that the $f_4$ function leads to a consistent description of hadronic cross-section data across multiple experiments, and that this distribution exhibits distinct $k_\perp$-dependent characteristics that set it apart from the traditional Bose-Einstein distribution. Furthermore, we found that $f_4$ exhibits a long-range $k_\perp$ oscillatory behavior, which cannot be captured by the Elliott-Ji distribution, and that this new distribution provides a more accurate description of data when compared to the Elliott-Ji approach.

The intricate relationship between protein knoting and folding remains poorly understood, with current knowledge unable to fully explain the folding processes of knotted proteins through the Bernal carbon copy method. Research has identified that these proteins can exist in complex, intertwined states, but it is unclear which paths of unfolding will occur. A new approach uses topological analysis and molecular dynamics simulations to systematically study the folding and unfolding of two knotted proteins. By examining the changes in spatial relationships during their simulations, researchers were able to distinguish true unfolding paths from artificial paths caused by carbon copy simulations. Using this approach, a set of genuine unfolding paths was identified for two specific knotted proteins, providing new insights into their folding processes. Furthermore, it was discovered that the spatial configurations of these proteins' binding sites are topologically distinct from those of non-knotted proteins, suggesting that specific binding sites may be necessary for the de-tangling process.

Early Dark Energy is a cosmological model that suggests a specific type of energy began operating very early in the universe's development. Researchers have previously established constraints on its parameters using the Planck satellite and the Baryonic Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey. This study refines those constraints based on an advanced statistical method that takes into account the uncertainties of the cosmological model itself. By applying this method to the same data, the team found that the parameters of Early Dark Energy were narrowed down to a particular range, which contradicts the model's predictions. In essence, the findings suggest that the model is not capable of explaining certain early universe phenomena.

This paper aims to determine the symplectic mapping class group of a specific torus blowup, specifically one with blowups over two points. We first establish that the symplectic mapping class group of a smooth symplectic manifold, particularly one with a simple topology, is equivalent to the group responsible for its large-scale geometric modifications. We then apply this understanding to identify the symplectic mapping class group of a blowup of a smooth, closed, and simply-connected manifold with a high-Kahler class. Furthermore, we extend this to quasi-positive curvature manifolds and find that the symplectic mapping class group of a blowup of a torus is isomorphic to the direct sum of the symplectic mapping class group of the original manifold and the symplectic mapping class group of a blowup of two points, with the latter being isomorphic to the integers two times zero.

The standard spontaneous symmetry breaking theorem in quantum field theory relies on a specific phenomenon: the appearance of a Nambu-Goldstone boson. However, this complex process can be broken down into two distinct components: the presence of spontaneous symmetry breaking and the appearance of a Nambu-Goldstone boson. In this review, we will challenge the conventional understanding of the second component by presenting a modified version of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem. In order for the appearance of a Nambu-Goldstone boson to occur, in addition to spontaneous symmetry breaking, it is necessary for there to be a low-energy long-range fluctuation mode. This requirement can be satisfied in a variety of ways, including but not limited to, the emergence of a Nambu-Goldstone boson. In fact, in some cases, the symmetry can be broken in a way that results in the formation of pairs of particles that are connected by a CKN symmetry matrix, leading to the creation of a corresponding number of Nambu-Goldstone bosons equal to the number of rows in the matrix. A theoretical model, the nonrelativistic scalar superconformal QCD, is used to illustrate the modified theorem in action. In this model, a pair of quark fields that are connected by a 3rd root of the square matrix break the conformal symmetry, giving rise to three Nambu-Goldstone bosons that represent a Longitudinal, Trans

Reasoning about complex scenarios is a key skill for testing knowledge and understanding of natural language. Although current assessments like Rationale Evaluation Systems focus on individual reasons, they may not capture the full depth of a situation's implications. In contrast, evaluating a system's ability to grasp a detailed, multi-faceted scenario - as might be presented in a long-form rationale - appears more challenging. To this end, we've developed a new assessment designed for understanding phrasal and sentential contexts, and have used it to examine the performance of large language models on a range of tasks. Our findings reveal that these models can successfully explain individual aspects of a situation, but struggle with more complex, interconnected scenarios. Moreover, our analysis indicates that the strong performance observed in other LAMER evaluations may be skewed by the prevalence of single-factor explanations.

In this study, the total colorings, equitable total colorings, and neighborhood sum distinguishing total colorings of specific types of circulant graphs are examined. The research focuses on circulant graphs constructed from the integers 2 and 3, using a particular combination method. It has been proven that certain subgroups of these circulant graphs can be colored using 2, 3, and 4 colors for their respective properties. Additionally, upper and lower bounds for the number of colors needed for the neighborhood sum distinguishing total colorings of these graphs have been established, with specific cases requiring 4 colors. The term "equitable" was mistakenly removed from the title in the initial publication; it has been corrected in this revised version.

The remote epitaxy technique offers a chance to overcome material-matching issues, but a lack of understanding about its fundamental mechanisms hinders widespread adoption. This study investigates the equilibrium between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy of Heusler films on graphene/sapphire substrates. By applying compressive strain to the graphene layer, the film growth mode can be switched between remote and pinhole epitaxy. A theoretical model suggests that the choice between these modes depends on the lattice mismatch between the film and the underlying graphene layer. A complementary study on film growth using a graphene layer on SiC substrates revealed that pinhole defects can act as nucleation sites for film growth, indicating that the film's energy state plays a crucial role in the remote epitaxy mechanism. As a result, we propose that the film's energy state is influenced by the presence of a graphene layer, which in turn allows for the realization of van der Waals epitaxy. These findings provide a framework for controlling the film growth mode and highlight the potential for using graphene layers to overcome material-matching issues in film growth.

This paper introduces a novel class of codes called $ \mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which incorporate elements from both $\mathbb{Z}_p$-linear and $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes. Specifically, this paper explores the rank and kernel size of these codes. Furthermore, specific conditions are established to determine both the dimension and kernel size of $ \mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes of arbitrary rank.

Hydraulic fracturing production is enhanced through the injection of crosslinking agents like xanthan, which also prevents concformance damage caused by filtration. However, the high cost of xanthan necessitates pinpoint injection profiling to ensure optimal use. This study aims to minimize xanthan cost under production constraints, given reservoir characteristics and flow data. A mathematical model is developed to determine the optimal injection profile, taking into account the relationship between xanthan injection rate and resulting production.

Learning from partially labeled data, particularly when each sample has multiple labels, is a challenging problem. In this paper, a proposed method uses a different approach, assigning a single label to a set of relevant samples, which are then inferred to have all the existing labels for that assigned label. A novel loss function and a proposed network architecture allow for the learning of these relationships between samples, which can be used to predict additional labels for each sample. Our experiments demonstrate that this method can improve performance on tasks with a large number of labels, and achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art models in low-label-scenarios.

This paper provides a novel upper bound for the energy associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, set within a periodic domain, as it evolves over time. The energy in question is defined by the integral of a specific function that combines squared values of the phase-field variable and its derivative, integrated across the domain at a given time. A specific strategy for updating the phase-field variable is used in this analysis. Under no additional assumptions about the initial conditions or the specific form of the function, an initial energy that diminishes over time can be demonstrated. This result indicates that, as the time parameter approaches zero, the energy upper bound approaches a limit that is equal to the initial energy.

The process of deriving a representation of the canonical commutation relation's Weyl algebra from a corresponding Wigner function is the key concept underlying this research. It is demonstrated that this process is essentially a categorification of one particular technique in algebraic geometry, known as the "geometric construction" for representations of commutative algebras. It is then shown that the abstract principles of this method can be applied to obtain the Weyl algebra representations in a broader algebraic context. Furthermore, it is proved that the algebraic geometry framework can be used to create tight frames of coherent states, and that it provides a new approach for classifying the unitary positive operators on Fock space.

The origin of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies remains an unsolved mystery. Using comprehensive magnetic field maps of the galaxies AGN disks, this paper suggests that high-energy gamma-rays could be produced when magnetic fields in these disks restrict the flow of electrons. This reaction typically requires protons to collide with abundant gas in the galactic bullets, forming pairs of electrons and positrons. However, when magnetic fields in the disks are constrained, this process can occur more efficiently, and the resulting gamma-rays might match the energy levels detected by the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope and the Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov Telescope.

This study examines the relationship between portfolio returns and the characteristics of investors, focusing on how returns are allocated across different sections of the market. Using a comprehensive database of 15 years of daily return and order data from the Tokyo Stock Exchange, researchers identified the long-term returns of individual stocks and then organized them into five categories of market capitalization. They found that higher-value stocks generally offer higher returns, but the returns on smaller stocks exhibit significant variation. In an analysis of 600,000 unique stocks over 15 years, the returns on smaller stocks were found to be consistently lower than expected returns in a market where the average stock has a market capitalization of $2 billion. This phenomenon persists across different market capitalization levels and is characterized by a long tail of underperforming stocks. In an effort to explain this "underperforming stock problem," researchers considered various factors, including the allocation of new listings, the characteristics of stocks, and the behavior of investors, but found no evidence to support these theories. This study provides a detailed analysis of the returns on individual stocks and the characteristics of the market, and its findings have implications for theories of capital market equilibrium and the allocation of resources.

Cardiovascular disease diagnosis through heart sound analysis is an effective method, however, this approach's success heavily relies on accurate heart sound categorization. In the presence of additive and convolutional noise within heart sound recordings, a comparative analysis of seven different noise reduction techniques and their impact on categorization was conducted. Following noise reduction, a convolutional neural network achieved high categorization accuracy even in noisy recordings, with an optimal technique resulting in a significant reduction in error rate.

The growing popularity of wearable devices and machine learning-based healthcare systems necessitates the development of scalable, secure, and privacy-preserving solutions. Due to the large amount of user data involved, training deep learning models directly on wearable device data becomes impractical. To address these challenges, we propose FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare that enables the effective training of models without compromising security and privacy. FedHealth leverages existing models as transfer knowledge, allowing it to handle diverse datasets effectively. Through experiments conducted on three real-world datasets, FedHealth achieved comparable performance to non-federated transfer learning methods, with notable improvements in cardiovascular risk assessment using a real-world dataset. Furthermore, FedHealth's ability to handle noisy and imbalanced data was demonstrated, along with the publication of the framework's source code.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies that go beyond mean-variance optimization, using a higher moment framework to characterize different approaches. It provides a detailed examination of various methods, including stochastic optimization, multi-objective, robust and robust multi-objective techniques, dynamic and asset tree models, and those that expand the mean-variance framework with higher moments.

In string compactifications, our universe's observations are shaped by the interactions between closed strings within a six-dimensional compact space with no net charge. The universe's uniformity can be attributed to the uniform distribution of these strings. The universe must be significantly older than what we observe for its strings to have had sufficient time to reach a thermal equilibrium that we can detect. However, if the universe is indeed this old, it should have already been dominated by these strings, contradicting our observations of a matter-dominated universe. This string age estimate gives us a de Broglie wavelength of approximately one kiloparsec for these strings, which translates to the universe's coincidence problem of why we exist at a particular moment in time. The universe must have a scale of around 10^18 megaparsecs to have reached the stage where these strings start leaving their cosmological horizon and cause the universe's matter domination. This scale matches the current cosmological constant problem, and we propose a future universe where the strings' departure from their horizons will trigger a second stage of cosmological expansion similar to the present day.

The term "Automation" in its general sense refers to the use of technology to automate repetitive tasks across all sectors. In the software development industry, this translates to using technology to automate tasks such as coding, testing, and debugging that are commonly performed manually. As a result, software development professionals can focus on higher-level tasks that require human creativity and ingenuity. Several software development technologies have been developed with this purpose in mind, including domain-specific languages, model-driven architecture, and rapid application development methods like Microsoft's Power Platform. However, despite these advancements, software development professionals still employ manual methods to accomplish tasks like data processing, validation, and transformation. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a new framework called AutoSoft, which utilizes machine learning and software development technologies to automate repetitive tasks in a way that allows human experts to focus on complex issues that require their unique skills.

This study explores a control issue where the costs incurred change abruptly at unknown points in time. The objective is to minimize the total cost, which becomes significantly more complex due to these sudden changes. The paper shows that the optimal strategy can be divided into distinct segments, with each segment optimally minimizing the cost in isolation. The paper also introduces a new method for determining the unknown change times by the optimal policy. This method allows the paper to derive a mathematical expression for the optimal policy and to discuss its stability. The paper shows that the optimal policy can lead to one of three possible outcomes: the costs remain constant and do not change at all, the costs change a finite number of times, or the costs change an infinite number of times. The paper also discusses the requirements needed for the costs to change a finite or infinite number of times. The paper was originally presented at the 12th IFAC Symposium on Control in Technical Systems, held on July 27-29, 2011, in Moscow, Russia.

To investigate the Leptoquark's properties, we analyze its production in pairs at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically in a scenario where the initial lepton and quark pairs have different energy levels. We focus on the case where the lepton and quark pairs have significantly different energies, and we choose the $l\tau$ and $e,u$ quark pair combinations for our analysis. In this context, we examine the impact of various assumptions about the Leptoquark's Higgs-like characteristics and its connection to the top quark's mass on our results. We also explore the effects of adjusting the Leptoquark's mass, as well as those of choosing the $l\tau,d$ or $e,s$ quark pair combinations. Our primary goal is to identify the set of experimental conditions required to determine the Leptoquark's mass independently of its other characteristics.

In the analysis of biological systems, time series data is often used to understand dynamic cellular processes. However, due to the high dimensionality of single-cell data, dimensionality reduction techniques are necessary for a comprehensive multidimensional analysis. Existing methods that combine temporal and spatial information through multiblock PCA are limited by their restrictive model assumptions. This study introduces a novel guided multiblock PCA approach that leverages prior knowledge of biological processes, as encoded in regulatory network models. By incorporating this guidance, the algorithm learns low-dimensional representations of time series data that capture the underlying biological dynamics across multiple genes within a single-cell culture. The guided approach is compared to an unsupervised method without prior biological knowledge, and the resulting low-dimensional embeddings are evaluated using a range of metrics, including clustering performance and visualization. The study also explores the utility of its approach for identifying cellular process dynamics by analyzing data from a mathematical simulator, as well as actual single-cell RNA sequencing data from a study on glucose metabolism. The results of this research demonstrate the value of guided multiblock PCA in analyzing high-dimensional time series data from a systems biology perspective.

The molecular gas in galaxies is generally subjected to low-temperature radiation, originating from the cooling gas and any active galactic nucleus present. This radiation causes the fine-structure lines of neutral atomic species to deviate from their expected low-temperature equilibrium with other molecular gas emission. By examining the [CII] line's relationship to the [CI] line, we can determine the excess [CII] emission's amount and its possible use as a galaxy's mass reservoir indicator, independent of gas temperature and chemistry assumptions. Based on observations of 11 galaxy samples, we find a robust correlation between excess [CII] emission and IR luminosity, as well as a distinct division between high-excess [CII] emission galaxies and those with low excess. The former group's characteristics align with starburst and AGN galaxy types, while the latter group includes spiral and massive early-type galaxies. These results demonstrate the potential for using [CII] over [CI] as a reservoir indicator in galaxy populations, and the excess [CII] emission can be utilized as a marker for identifying galaxies with extreme starbursts or AGN activity hidden from optical observations.

We investigate the implications of sectoring the TeV physics into two distinct sectors, assuming that the standard sector and the b-flavored sector operate independently. We explore the implications of this assumption on the observed anomalies in the LHC data and show that under this framework, the observed anomalies in the $K^0$ and $B$ meson systems can be simultaneously explained for a specific range of the mass scale $\sim 2-3$ TeV. Furthermore, this model predicts a specific range of masses for the $B$ anomalies and the LHC data on a $W$ boson partner, and we find that the latter is in tension with the predicted results.

Xia leveraged the Hamming distance to study the sequence reconstruction problem.
He investigated a specific case where a permutation of elements from the set {1,2,...,k} is evaluated after being arranged in a particular order.
Rather than using the standard Hamming distance, Xia modified it to account for the effects of the permutation's initial and terminal elements.
With this modification, the standard bound of 2k consecutive observations was shown to be insufficient for reconstructing the underlying sequence.
Instead, Xia established conditions under which the sequence could be determined with either 3k or 3k-1 consecutive observations.

This study proposes a novel approach to identifying musical instruments across various categories using a limited dataset. Our method leverages hierarchical structures to model the relationships between instruments and uses a novel contrastive loss function to train a prototype-based network with a fixed transformer for pattern recognition. This is the first attempt to apply such a combination to this task. We achieved outstanding performance on the MUSDB18 dataset, using only 32 examples per category for training and obtained remarkable results on larger datasets with only a few examples per class. Our code is available online for review and improvement.

Academic researchers who read multiple papers still struggle to keep a broad
overview of a field. This challenge is compounded by the growing number of
research papers being published every year. One key to addressing this issue is
to develop a way to efficiently query a corpus of papers for key information.
However, current evaluation metrics for machine comprehension tasks do not
adequately assess a model's ability to learn a corpus's underlying structure and
to generalize beyond the specific questions it was asked. To overcome these
limitations, we have created a new dataset consisting of 10,000 questions posed
to 2,000 research papers drawn from three distinct domains. We have also
introduced a set of guidelines for framing knowledge-seeking questions as multiple
choice answers, as opposed to open-ended questions. Our results indicate that
even models with extensive training on the underlying corpus still struggle to
achieve better than change-blind performance. Notably, these models performed no
better on questions they were trained on than on those they were not. Our data
also reveal that the best performing models were those with limited training on the
underlying corpus, with an average performance of 31.3% on the full dataset.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in elliptical orbits. This study focuses on the creation of artificial signals that replicate these waves and can be used in mock PTA data. The team has developed a method to generate these artificial signals at varying levels of precision, either using highly detailed post-Newtonian representations or less detailed but faster computational forms. This study assesses the trade-offs between signal accuracy and computational efficiency, with implications for signal creation that could inform future mock data generation in PTA experiments.

We examine the velocity process derived from the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) on a one-dimensional discrete space, specifically considering discrete time. In a closed system, we analyze the stationary velocities, showing that they form a Markov-renewal process with independent increments. In an open system with constant input and output rates, we characterize the stationary velocities as well as their rates of change. We also investigate the total displacement process of particles entering/leaving the system and establish relationships with the velocity process. Finally, we discuss the long-term behavior of the velocity process in cases where the rate of particle movement exceeds the system's capacity.

The ongoing battle against the present SARS-CoV-2 epidemic serves as a reminder that epidemics pose a constant threat to global health, necessitating continuous preparedness and effective countermeasures. Understanding the basic principles of mathematical modeling can provide valuable insights into the process of modeling epidemics, as well as the role that modeling can play in disease control and management. This article aims to offer a non-technical overview of compartmental models, as well as their applications in the present SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, using examples from Italy and Brazil.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. We then investigate the Tsallis q-entropies of the Majorana fermion and its relation to the linear external potential. We investigate this relationship both analytically and numerically. We found that the linear external potential affects the particle's behavior, affecting both its entropy characteristics. We propose the name "Majorana distribution" for the distribution resulting from this analysis. We also found that the linear external potential results in non-trivial, real roots for the particle's position and momentum. These roots are dependent on the particle's mass and the strength of the external potential. We also investigated the Tsallis q-statistics of the Majorana fermion, including its distribution, influence on the thermodynamic potential, and relationship to the linear external potential. We found that the linear external potential has a significant impact on the particle's distribution, influencing both its average and variance.

Acronyms and abbreviations are employed to condense lengthy phrases comprising
various elements like names, titles, and combinations of both. While they are
efficient in expression, they can introduce confusion when used in place of the
full phrase. Over time, the original phrase may be forgotten, leading to
disambiguation difficulties. To address this challenge, the original phrase needs
to be retrieved from memory, often occupying a spot in short-term memory where
information is temporarily held. This processing demands cognitive resources,
potentially hindering comprehension and memory recall. To mitigate this, it's
common to break down long phrases into shorter acronyms, a practice observed
across various languages. As such, effective acronym disambiguation is crucial
for clear communication and comprehension. Humans employ various strategies to
achieve this, such as placing the acronym after the associated phrase, using
capitalization, and incorporating a definition. However, these cues can be
insufficient or even misleading, highlighting the need for a systematic
approach. To facilitate both human and artificial understanding, we introduce
MadDog, a web-based acronym disambiguation platform that allows users to
create, manage, and share acronym lists. These lists comprise definitions,
associated phrases, and the corresponding acronyms, along with indicators of
potential ambiguity. MadDog provides a tool for humans to understand and
clarify ambiguous acronyms and a resource for machine learning models to

We have theoretically analyzed the interplay between photoassociation and stimulated emission in a system of two spin-polarized atoms and one atom-molecule interaction system in the long-wavelength limit of far-off-resonance conditions. A key factor influencing this interplay is the one-dimensional character of the system's physics, which can be controlled by a laser field to atom-molecule conversion or vice versa. A crucial aspect of this control is the two-dimensional projection of the system's initial or final state. A critical condition for this control must be met and can be satisfied by adjusting the intensity of an interacting laser field. A notable outcome of this analysis is the prediction of a high efficiency of three-body recombination processes on certain antinodes of a laser field. A key factor contributing to this efficiency is the one-dimensional character of the system's dynamics, which can be understood as a result of the laser field's action, leading to increased recombination rates under certain conditions and resulting in significant enhancements of recombination rates over typical values. A further implication of this analysis is the prediction of a high efficiency of three-body recombination processes on certain antinodes of a laser field, which could potentially result in significant increases in recombination rates in other dimensions. A key factor contributing to this efficiency is the one-dimensional character of the system's dynamics, which can be understood as a result of the laser field's action, leading to increased recombination rates under certain conditions and resulting in significant enhancements of recombination rates over

Previous studies have leveraged DNA storage due to its exceptionally low costs, potentially surpassing conventional storage media in price-performance ratio. Research in this area has so far focused primarily on fundamental read and write operations. This work expands on previous studies by exploring two critical functionalities in any data management system: complex query hierarchies and data updates. In DNA storage, these functions are crucial for implementing essential commands like sorting and backing up databases. To achieve this, we developed a DNA storage schema consisting of two layers, where query data is stored on a parallel strand to enable efficient hybrid read-write operations. To validate our approach, we conducted a sample database update using MySQL and compared the results with conventional hard disk storage, showing that our DNA storage system supports updates and query hierarchies while maintaining a significantly low error rate of less than $10^{-3}$.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of the bulk and edge/surface states. In momentum space, the most distinctive feature of these materials is the topologically protected line that divides the momentum space into distinct areas with opposite Chern numbers. Although extensively studied in two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) systems, the understanding of these lines in 2D momentum space is limited. Recently, research in 2D topological insulators has expanded to include quasi-2D systems and has revealed the existence of nodal lines. This paper reviews recent developments in 2D topological insulators, focusing on quasi-2D materials, graphene, and photonic systems, and discusses various approaches used to observe these phenomena. Furthermore, this paper discusses the various methods employed to create these systems, including molecular assembly, van der Waals stacking, layer-by-layer construction, molecular functionalization, and laser writing.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the type and area of the tumor.  However, analyzing MRI scans can be time and labor intensive for radiologists.  Developing automated systems for tumor classification and segmentation is now the focus.  In this study, we develop a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI data to classify and segment brain tumors.  The model is trained on the BRATS2019 dataset and outperforms existing systems according to evaluation metrics.  Specifically, it achieves high Dice coefficients (0.963, 0.955, 0.955, 0.945) and low Hausdorff distances (0.849, 0.784, 0.784, 0.784) for per-tumour, per-ventricle, etmoid and nodule segmentation respectively, as well as high accuracy (0.97) for classification.  The model's success is attributed to its ability to focus on relevant features and ignore irrelevant ones, thereby reducing the computation required and minimizing the impact of MRI noise.
